title: The 48-Hour Record Request Is Coming: Broker Transparency Decisions While the Rule Sits at OIRA
summary: FMCSA's broker transparency proposal is under White House review. Decide now what your 371.3 record holds and how you will produce it in 48 hours.
body_markdown:
A carrier you have used for two years disputes a $400 chargeback on a dry van load out of the Midwest. The receiver signed a clean delivery receipt. Your team withheld the money anyway, because the shipper short-paid your invoice and the claim note says "late delivery." The carrier's owner sends a written request under 49 CFR 371.3 for the transaction record.


Now someone has to build it. The rate confirmation is a PDF in a rep's inbox. The original tender came in by EDI. The detention approval lives in a text thread. The shipper invoice and the carrier settlement come out of two different exports, and the quick-pay fee shows up as a net number with no line item. Nobody can say, with confidence, what the shipper paid for detention versus what the carrier received, or when either payment cleared.


That is not a compliance problem yet. Under today's rule it is an awkward afternoon. Under the rule FMCSA is drafting, it could be a missed 48-hour deadline.


## Where the rule actually stands (as of Oct 14, 2026)


The rulemaking is "Transparency in Property Broker Transactions," RIN 2126-AC63, docket FMCSA-2023-0257. The short history matters because it tells you what is likely to survive.


-


**Aug 19, 2020:** FMCSA sought comment on two petitions to strengthen 371.3 (85 FR 51145). It received 1,391 comments on them.


-


**Mar 16, 2023:** FMCSA granted both petitions. A day later it denied a competing petition from broker interests to eliminate the right to review.


-


**Nov 20, 2024:** The NPRM published (89 FR 91648). Comments closed Jan 21, 2025.


-


**Feb 18 to Mar 20, 2025:** The comment period reopened for 30 days (90 FR 9702). Trade coverage puts the total across both windows at roughly 7,000 comments.


-


**2026:** Instead of finalizing, DOT chose to write a supplemental proposal. The Unified Agenda targeted May 2026, then July 2026. Both passed.


-


**Aug 27, 2026:** The supplemental proposal went to the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA). It is listed as a proposed rule, not economically significant, with no legal deadline.


-


**Sept 17, 2026:** OIRA held an EO 12866 meeting on the file with a small-business transportation group.


-


**Oct 14, 2026:** OIRA's pending-review list still shows the rule under review. Nothing new has published in the Federal Register.


EO 12866 reviews generally run up to 90 days, which would land around late November, and they can be extended. When OIRA clears it, the text publishes and a new comment period opens. A final rule is at least one more full cycle away.


So the current 371.3 still governs. Brokers must keep a record of each transaction for 3 years. The record must show the consignor, the originating carrier with its registration number, the bill of lading or freight bill number, the broker's compensation and who paid it, any non-brokerage services, and freight charges collected with the date paid to the carrier. Each party to the transaction has the right to review it.


## What the 2024 proposal would change


We have not seen the supplemental text. But the 2024 NPRM is the best map of FMCSA's thinking, and it proposed four things:


1.


**Electronic records.** Kept in a format consistent with FMCSA's electronic document rules, so a broker cannot answer a request by offering a visit to the home office.


2.


**Fuller contents.** Every charge and fee tied to the shipment (freight charges, surcharges, accessorials) with amount, description, date of payment, and payer, plus any penalties or claims assessed. It would drop the old brokerage versus non-brokerage distinction.


3.


**An affirmative duty.** Access reframed from a party's "right to review" into a regulatory obligation on the broker to provide.


4.


**48 hours.** Records delivered electronically within 48 hours of a request from any party to the transaction.


Two things it did not do are just as important. It did not require automatic disclosure after every load. And it did not ban waiver clauses outright. FMCSA said no statute expressly makes the right non-waivable, then argued that recasting access as a compliance duty makes waivers "largely moot." It also said confidentiality clauses that limit disclosure to non-parties remain fine.


The supplemental could move on any of these points. The decisions below hold up either way.


## Decision 1: Define the transaction record before a regulator does


Most shops have a load record. Few have a transaction record. The difference is the money on both sides and the history of how it changed.


Write down, internally, what your 371.3 record contains for one load. At minimum:


-


The tender and the shipper rate, plus every shipper-side accessorial and adjustment


-


The carrier rate confirmation and every carrier-side accessorial approved after it


-


Carrier identity as verified at booking: legal name, registration number, and who actually hauled


-


Bill of lading or freight bill number, and the proof of delivery


-


Each payment in and out, with amount, date, and payer


-


Every deduction: chargebacks, claims, penalties, quick-pay or advance fees


-


Notes explaining any shipper short-pay that flowed down to the carrier


The proposal's own example is instructive. One commenter described a broker billing the shipper detention after the first hour at $50 an hour while paying the carrier only after four hours at $35. Whatever you think of that spread, under the proposed itemization both sides of it would sit in the same document. Decide now whether your policies survive being read side by side.


## Decision 2: Name an owner and a clock


A 48-hour clock does not tolerate "whoever booked the load." Pick one function to own production. In most brokerages that is billing or carrier settlement, not sales, because they already reconcile both sides of the money.


Then define the workflow:


-


**Intake.** One monitored channel for record requests, logged with a timestamp. Ambiguity about when the clock started is a bad argument to be making.


-


**Verification.** Confirm the requester is a party to that transaction. The duty runs to parties, not to anyone who emails.


-


**Assembly.** Pull from the system of record, not from inboxes.


-


**Review.** A short check against confidentiality terms with the shipper.


-


**Delivery and proof.** Send electronically and keep evidence of when.


Run a drill this quarter. Pick ten completed loads at random, including two with claims and two with quick-pay, and time how long it takes to produce a clean record. If the answer is measured in days, you know your real exposure.


## Decision 3: Assume margin visibility and negotiate accordingly


The rule does not set or cap margins, and FMCSA said so plainly. It also said it could not rule out carriers using the information to negotiate better rates over time. Plan for that version.


If a carrier can see that the shipper paid $3,100 and the carrier got $2,550, the conversation shifts from "is this rate fair" to "what did you do for the $550." Brokers with a defensible answer (claims handling, payment terms faster than the shipper's, contracted rates that run negative in a spiking spot market) should be ready to say it. Brokers whose answer is "we were the only one who knew the shipper" should think hard about which lanes depend on that.


The flip side: brokers that pay carriers in days while the shipper pays in 30 or more are carrying real float risk. The proposed date-of-payment fields make that visible too. Transparency can work in your favor if your record tells the story.


## Decision 4: Treat waiver clauses as a risk, not a shield


Many broker-carrier agreements still contain a clause waiving the carrier's right to review. Today, whether that waiver holds is a contract and litigation question. The 2024 proposal declined to ban it outright but tried to move the duty out of the contract entirely, and FMCSA stated that 49 U.S.C. 14101(b), the provision commonly cited for waivers, generally does not reach brokers.


Practical moves while the text is pending:


-


Inventory which carrier agreements contain waivers and which shipper agreements contain confidentiality terms that might conflict with a records duty.


-


Have counsel draft a fallback clause that keeps confidentiality toward non-parties without relying on the waiver.


-


Stop treating the waiver as the reason you do not need a clean record. If the supplemental tightens the duty, the waiver will not cover the gap.


## Decision 5: Put accessorials, deductions, and payment fees in fields, not notes


This is where most records fall apart. Each of these needs a structured home with amount, date, reason, and documentation:


-


**Accessorials.** Detention, layover, lumper, TONU, driver assist. Record the shipper-billed and carrier-paid amounts as separate lines, with the approval trail.


-


**Chargebacks and claims deductions.** The NPRM notes carriers' complaints about chargebacks after clean delivery receipts and about cross-collateralized holds on other loads. A deduction without a linked claim document is the line item most likely to start a dispute.


-


**Penalties.** Late delivery or service failures passed down from the shipper, tied to the shipper's actual deduction.


-


**Quick-pay and advance fees.** Show the gross rate, the fee, and the net paid as three lines. A net-only settlement is the fastest way to look like you hid something you did not.


-


**Factoring.** When a carrier assigns receivables, record the payee you actually paid and the date. Paying the wrong party is a separate problem that a clean record makes easy to prove or disprove.


## Decision 6: Make verification part of the record


FMCSA's NPRM asked whether carriers policing transactions with transparency data could push illegal brokering out of the market. Whatever the answer, double brokering disputes come down to records: who you tendered to, what identity checks you ran, and who actually showed up at the dock.


Capture the verification you performed at booking (authority status, registration number, contact confirmation, any re-tender) as part of the transaction, timestamped. If a load was re-brokered without your consent, the record is your evidence. If your own carrier is accused, the same record is your defense.


## Exposure by business model


Model


Owes records


Demands records


Biggest exposure now


Asset carrier


No (on carrier freight)


Yes, from brokers it hauls for


Accepting waivers and losing leverage in chargeback disputes


Pure broker


Yes, on every load


Rarely


Scattered records and unexplained deductions on a 48-hour clock


Hybrid (asset plus brokerage arm)


Yes, on brokered loads


Yes, as a carrier


Inconsistent policies between divisions that each side can quote back


Hybrids carry the sharpest version of this. Your fleet division may be asking other brokers for records the same week your brokerage division is resisting the same request. A carrier you broker to will notice. Pick one standard and apply it in both directions.


## The real work is configuration


Every freight business structures its deals differently. Some price accessorials into the line haul, some bill them separately, some pay detention on a schedule, and some share a percentage. No regulation will tell you how your business works. What it will do is ask you to prove it, quickly.


The shops that will handle a 48-hour request calmly are the ones whose statuses, approval steps, permissions, and billing fields already match how they actually do business, so that every accessorial approval, deduction, and payment lands in a structured place as it happens. Then the record is not something you assemble under pressure. It is a report you run.


Do that work while the text sits at OIRA. When it publishes, you will be reading it to see what to adjust, not what to build.


## FAQ


### Is the FMCSA broker transparency rule in effect?


No. As of Oct 14, 2026, FMCSA's supplemental proposal is still under OIRA review and has not published, so the existing 49 CFR 371.3 still governs. Publication would open a new comment period before any final rule.


### What does 49 CFR 371.3 require today?


Brokers must keep a record of each transaction for 3 years, and each party to the transaction has the right to review it. The record covers the consignor, the carrier and its registration number, the bill of lading or freight bill number, broker compensation and payer, non-brokerage services, and freight charges collected with the date paid to the carrier.


### Would brokers have to send records automatically after every load?


Not under the 2024 proposal. It required production within 48 hours of a request, not automatic disclosure, though the supplemental text has not been released and could differ.


### Are waiver clauses in broker-carrier contracts still enforceable?


That is currently a contract and litigation question. The 2024 proposal did not ban waivers outright but recast record access as a regulatory duty on brokers, which FMCSA said would make waivers largely moot.


### Should quick-pay fees and chargebacks appear in the transaction record?


Yes, if you want a record that holds up. The 2024 proposal called for itemizing all charges, fees, and penalties tied to a shipment with dates and payers, so a gross rate, the fee, and the net payment should each be visible.


### What should a hybrid asset and brokerage company do first?


Set one records standard for both divisions. The same company will both request and owe records, and inconsistent policies are easy for counterparties to point out.
